title: Childhood Laryngeal Dystonia Following Bilateral Globus Pallidus Abnormality: A Case Study and Review of Literature
case_prompt:
A 7½-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of balance disturbances, incoordination of extraocular muscles during walking, dysfunctional gag reflex and swallowing, vocal tremor, monotone speech, and weakness of the masticatory muscles. His motor development had been delayed. There was no family history of laryngeal dystonia; his grandfather had late-life Parkinson’s disease. He had no history of birth asphyxia or cyanosis, and psychological evaluation revealed normal cognition.

Routine laboratory tests, including serum electrolytes, blood glucose, liver function, and kidney function, were normal. Urine and blood chromatography showed no abnormal bands or amino acid elevations. Plasma copper (90 μg/dl) and lactate (9.6 mg/dl) levels were within normal limits, with no evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction.

On examination, he was alert with normal language comprehension, naming, and repetition. Cranial nerves were intact: pupils, visual fields, and funduscopic exam were normal; Kayser–Fleischer rings were absent. He had extraocular incoordination during walking. Facial sensation and movements were normal. The palate and uvula elevated symmetrically; tongue protruded midline. Deep tendon reflexes were hyperactive with bilateral Babinski signs and persistence of a biting reflex. Cerebellar testing was normal. Masticatory muscles were weak, and the gag reflex was hypersensitive.

Brain MRI showed bilateral signal abnormalities in the globus pallidus: axial FLAIR images demonstrated hypointensity with central hyperintensity, and sagittal T2-weighted images confirmed a hyperintense medial portion. The remainder of the brain, ventricular system, brainstem, and cervical cord appeared normal. CT head showed normal gray–white matter differentiation and no lesions. Brainstem auditory evoked potentials, somatosensory evoked potentials, and flash visual evoked potentials all had normal wave morphology, amplitudes, and latencies.

Audio recording and perceptual assessment of a 10-minute speech sample revealed breathiness, roughness, vocal tremor, monotone pitch, and breathy breaks. Maximum phonation time averaged 5 seconds.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Inherited or acquired metabolic disorders were excluded because “there were no bands in the urine and no detectable increase in any particular amino acid in the plasma sample, in favor of any inherited or acquired metabolic disorders.”  
2. Mitochondrial disorders were considered but ruled out since “there was no evidence of mitochondrial disorders. The plasma lactate level was in normal range (9.6 mg/dl).”  
3. Wilson disease was excluded based on absence of Kayser–Fleischer rings and normal copper levels: “Because of the lack of The Kayser–Fleischer ring and the normal range of copper plasma level, Wilson’s disease was not considered as a diagnosis for this patient.”  
4. Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA), particularly Hallervorden–Spatz syndrome, remained a possibility but could not be confirmed because “this requires a genetic study for the detection of the PANK-2 gene; however, his genetic study findings were not available.”
